seed.topicSeed: a train-station cafe in Hamburg; a mother-in-law and a new bride about an object that belonged to someone gone

g.passage:
I watched Katharina unwrap the brooch
beside a cup of coffee going cold,
the Hamburg trains exhaling on the platform
like tired men setting down their coats.
Her husband's, she said, pinned each winter
to the collar he wore for every leaving.
My hands, a bride's hands, were not certain
what a newcomer is owed of the dead,
or whether I had any right to touch it.
But she slid it over the marble tabletop
slowly, the way one offers bread to a sparrow,
and smiled the small smile of a woman
who has practiced letting go in private.
I held it until the metal warmed,
until it seemed, almost, to hold me back,
and Katharina's hand rested on my wrist.
Outside, a whistle; somewhere a door;
the waiter brushing crumbs into his palm.

g.passage: By the time Parvin unlocked the studio, the Tehran afternoon had already gone amber in the dusty skylight. Pearl and I had not stood in this room together since our last season on the stage, when we were young enough to rehearse lines while our aunt threw bowls at the wheel behind us. Her glazes still lined the shelves, blue as the costumes we used to borrow without asking. I laughed when Pearl found a cracked cup with both our initials scratched into its foot, and for a moment we were girls again, trading whispered cues. Yet the buyer's letter sat folded on the kiln, and neither of us had read it twice. Pearl ran her thumb along the cup's rough edge. I opened a window, and somewhere below, a vendor called out the price of pomegranates.

g.passage: I boarded Albert's barge on the Irwell expecting to stay ten minutes. Thirty years earlier he had torn my essay in half before the whole class, and I had carried that sound with me ever since. Now he moved slowly between coils of rope, offering tea in a chipped mug, and I kept my coat buttoned and my answers short. He did not apologize. Instead he showed me a shoebox of student papers he had kept, and mine was near the top, taped carefully along its tear. I set the mug down without drinking. Still, when he struggled with the stove, I reached over and lit it for him, and I did not leave when the ten minutes were up. Gulls settled on the roof of the cabin, and the water knocked against the hull.

g.passage: Dongsik mended nets on the Busan pier while Rania read Korean aloud from a child's workbook. When she stumbled over a word for sorry, he corrected her without looking up, then repeated it twice, more softly, as if testing it himself. She had come all this way after her father's funeral, carrying a letter Dongsik had written to his son years ago and never mailed. Every evening she asked whether she could read it to him yet, and every evening he said her vowels were still too American. Tonight, though, he slid the envelope across the crate between them and tapped one line with a tar-stained finger. Read only this part, he said. Rania bent over the paper, sounding out each syllable. Beyond them, a trawler backed slowly out of its berth, its lights blinking green and red.
g.question: Based on the text, which choice best describes the relationship between Dongsik and Rania?

g.passage: Nobody waits at a cemetery gate by accident. Tamika had been leaning on the iron bars for an hour when Ottavio's rental car finally pulled off the Delta road, dust rising behind it. He had moved north the spring her mother got sick, and she had stayed to do the nursing, the paperwork, the long nights. She did not mention any of that. She only said he had missed the service by two days. Ottavio nodded, took off his sunglasses, and handed her an envelope thick with receipts: every bill from the hospital, paid in his name, which she had never been told about. Tamika stared at them for a long time before tucking the envelope into her purse and taking his arm. Out past the gate, cotton fields ran flat to the tree line under a white sky.

g.passage: Warm yeast, wet flour, and the hiss of the tandoor filled the Samarkand bakery long before dawn. Darius arrived each morning at four, though Aydin paid him only for six, and he swept the floor before she could ask. Neither of them spoke of the winter her husband had lent Darius's mother the money for a surgery, or of the fact that it had never been repaid. When he lifted the heaviest trays, she pretended not to notice. When she slipped an extra round of bread into his satchel, wrapped in a cloth embroidered with her husband's initials, he pretended the same. Once, he began to say something about his mother, and Aydin handed him a sack of sesame seeds before he could finish. Through the window, the blue dome of the mosque slowly took shape against the brightening sky.
g.question: Based on the text, which choice best describes the relationship between Aydin and Darius?

g.passage: We waited on the bench nearest the Havana ferry ramp, Father Emiliano in his faded cassock and I, Cleotilde, with a ticket my cousin had bought me to leave by morning. A thick mooring rope lay coiled at our feet, salt-stiff and frayed where it had rubbed the pier for years. I had not been to Mass in a decade, and I told him so, as if he did not already know. He only nodded at the rope. Every boat that docks here, he said, gets tied with that same line, and it never seems to break. When the gangway lowered, a deckhand looped the rope around a post, and the ferry strained against it, groaning, held fast. I folded my ticket into a smaller square. Even after I stood, my eyes kept returning to that worn rope, knotted so many times it had stopped looking like rope at all.

the ties to home and faith that still hold Cleotilde as she leaves.

g.passage: Milena held the dustpan while her mother swept, as she had every Saturday since she was nine. Marlon's barbershop on Brīvības Street closed at six, and her mother, who had cut hair there for twenty years, never let anyone else sweep up. Tonight they were supposed to be choosing wedding napkins, and the catalog lay open on a barber chair, but the broom kept moving in its old pattern: under the mirrors, around the coat rack, toward the door. Brown curls, gray tufts, a child's blond fringe. You'll have your own floors soon, her mother said, not looking up. Milena tipped the pan into the bin. Then she took the broom from her mother's hands and finished the last corner herself, the way she had seen it done a thousand times. Marlon, counting the till, pretended not to watch. Her mother sat down at last and turned a page of the catalog.

g.explanation: 청소는 밀레나가 아홉 살 때부터 매주 토요일 엄마와 함께해 온 의식으로 소개되고, 결혼 준비 중에도 비질은 옛 패턴대로 이어진다. 엄마가 '곧 너만의 바닥이 생길 것'이라고 말한 뒤 밀레나가 비를 받아 엄마가 하던 방식대로 마지막 구석을 마친다. 이를 종합하면 비질은 삶이 바뀌는 순간에도 두 사람을 이어 주는 공유된 의식이므로 C가 정답이다. A는 탈출하고 싶은 일로, B는 결혼 거부로, D는 마를론의 기준으로 잘못 해석했다.

g.passage:
Three rules of the theater in the off-season:
no films, no tickets, no one asks why you came.
Nandi sat in row nine in his pressed uniform,
his transfer papers folded inside his cap,
and Neema, his sister, swept popcorn husks
from a Nairobi rainy season months gone.
Above them the screen hung blank and white,
a field no one had walked across yet.
He had watched worse things than films on other walls.
She flicked the projector on by accident,
and light poured out with nothing in it,
just dust turning slowly in the beam.
He did not ask her to switch it off.
He stood, walked to the stage, and laid his palm
flat against the empty screen,
as if it were warm, as if it might hold
whatever he decided to put there.
Neema kept sweeping. The cap stayed on the seat.
g.question: In the text, the blank screen most likely represents
options: the violent memories that Nandi cannot stop replaying in his mind.
the loneliness of the theater during the long off-season months.
the films that Neema wishes the theater could afford to show again.

g.passage: Years later, at a crowded wedding hall in Rotterdam, I saw a paper crane tucked behind a place card, and I thought at once of Grant. He had been my night patient for three weeks on the cardiac ward, and every evening when I came to check his monitors, there was a new crane folded from a menu card on his tray. The other nurses teased me that he wanted something: a larger dose, an extra blanket, my phone number. I waited for the request. It never came. On his last night he asked only whether I had kept them, and when I said yes, all nineteen, he closed his eyes and smiled. I left the cranes on my windowsill for years, where they faded in the sun but never fell. At the wedding, I picked up the one by my plate and held it as the music started.
g.question: In the text, the paper cranes most likely represent
options: a gratitude Grant offered without expecting anything back.
a quiet request that Grant was too embarrassed to say aloud.
the boredom Grant felt during his long nights in the hospital.
the playful teasing that Freja endured from the other nurses.
g.explanation: 동료 간호사들은 학들이 무언가를 바라는 신호라고 놀렸지만, 화자가 기다린 요청은 끝내 오지 않았다. 마지막 밤에도 그랜트는 학을 간직했는지만 묻고 미소 지었으며, 화자는 학들을 오랫동안 창턱에 두었다. 이를 이어 보면 학은 대가를 바라지 않은 감사의 표시이므로 A가 정답이다. B는 동료들의 의심을 그대로 따른 오답이고, C의 지루함과 D의 놀림은 학의 의미를 소재 수준에서만 해석했다.

g.passage: On the evenings after we closed the shop early, Hala and I took the old ball down to the dirt field behind the Marrakesh tannery. Its leather had split along one seam, and every week Hala stitched it again with waxed thread from our father's spool, though a new ball cost less than an afternoon of his time. We never spoke of the ledger, of the rent three months late, or of the doctor's letter about our father that I had hidden in the drawer under the receipts. We just passed the ball back and forth while the call to prayer rose over the walls. It was heavier each time, the stitches thicker, the shape a little more lopsided. Still neither of us suggested buying another. When it rolled into the shadows near the goalposts, Hala jogged after it, and I waited, the dust turning pink in the last of the light.
g.question: In the text, the repeatedly stitched ball most likely represents

the brothers' unspoken effort to keep a failing life intact together.

g.explanation: 형제는 장부나 밀린 임대료, 숨겨 둔 의사 편지에 대해 말하지 않으면서 매주 터진 공을 다시 꿰매 함께 차고, 공은 점점 무거워지고 비뚤어지지만 누구도 새 공을 사자고 하지 않는다. 이 공은 망가져 가는 가게와 가족의 현실을 말없이 붙들고 버티는 두 사람의 노력과 겹쳐진다. 따라서 B가 정답이다. A는 축구라는 소재만, C는 '새 공이 더 싸다'는 서술과 어긋나고, D는 아버지의 실을 쓴다는 세부를 과장했다.

g.passage: Who gives a widow a shovel for her seventy-fifth birthday? Zawadi had asked herself that for a week, ever since Theo arrived with the long box tied in green ribbon. Since his grandfather's death she had not left the flat, and she suspected the gift was a polite way of telling her to stop sitting in the dark and find some useful chore. So the shovel stood in the corner of the kitchen like an accusation, and each time she passed it, she looked away. On Sunday Theo came back and took her by the arm to the community garden above the Marseille harbor. In the far bed, under a fig tree, a small wooden sign carried his grandfather's name. He kept this plot for forty years, Theo said. Nobody else should dig it. Zawadi stood very still, then held out her hand for the shovel he had carried up the hill.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “like an accusation” most nearly suggests that the shovel
options: was too heavy and awkward for Zawadi to use comfortably.
reminded Zawadi of the tools her husband once kept in the flat.

g.passage: Josiah had bought fish from Ephraim every Friday for two years and had never once seen the old man smile. Everyone on Mill Street said he was a miser who shorted his scales and cursed at children. So Josiah nearly dropped his notebook the Tuesday night he walked into the adult English class at the Ohio language school and found Ephraim at the chalkboard, patiently drilling six new arrivals on the names of vegetables. The teacher explained afterward that Ephraim had come to the town forty years ago knowing no English, and that he had taught the night class for free ever since, on one condition: that no one at the market ever learn of it. His temper, she said, was a fence he had built himself, high enough that no one would come to thank him. Josiah watched the old man erase the board in long, careful strokes.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a fence he had built himself” most nearly suggests that Ephraim's temper is
options: a habit he acquired from the harsh customers at the market.
a sign of the frustration he feels while teaching new arrivals.
a flaw that his neighbors have unfairly exaggerated over time.
a barrier he keeps up on purpose to hold gratitude away.
g.explanation: 에프라임은 수업을 무료로 가르치면서 시장 사람들이 절대 알지 못하게 하라는 조건을 걸었고, 교사는 그의 성질이 아무도 고맙다고 찾아오지 못할 만큼 높게 쌓은 '울타리'라고 말한다. 따라서 이 비유는 감사를 멀리하려고 그가 일부러 세워 둔 장벽을 뜻하므로 D가 정답이다. A는 '스스로 지었다'는 점과 어긋나고, B는 그가 인내심 있게 가르친다는 서술과 맞지 않는다. C는 이웃의 소문을 다루지만 비유가 강조하는 의도적 선택을 놓쳤다.

g.passage:
We were twelve in a cabin outside Dhaka
the winter snow came, absurd and soft,
sealing the road the festival van would use.
Arjun had promised word by evening:
whether the orchestra would play in the capital
or fold its music stands for good.
Meera, the youngest, held her violin unopened
in its case across her knees.
No one rehearsed. No one ate the rice.
By dusk the silence tuned itself to a single string,
and every face leaned toward the radio
the way a bow leans toward a note.
Arjun paced from the stove to the window,
his baton tucked behind one ear,
forgetting it was there.
Meera unlatched the case at last,
not to play, only to see the wood,
while snow kept falling past the glass.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “the silence tuned itself to a single string” most nearly suggests that

g.passage: Katerina drove the number 12 bus past the harbor in Thessaloniki every morning, and every morning Eda boarded at the stop beside the shoe repair stall. One spring she stepped on carrying a pair of men's brown oxfords, the heels worn to a slant. Her husband had died in January. She had brought the shoes to the cobbler three times, she told Katerina, asking him to replace the soles, then the laces, then the stitching along the toe. Each time he did the work without complaint, and each time she took them home and set them by the door, where no one would wear them. Mending them, Eda said, was like stitching a new sentence onto a closed book. Katerina said nothing and waited at the green light a moment longer than she needed to, so Eda could sit down. Then she pulled away from the curb into the traffic along the sea.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “stitching a new sentence onto a closed book” most nearly suggests

a task that Eda finds tedious and wishes she could abandon.

g.passage: Rumors travel faster than ferries. I learned that the autumn I clerked for Ingeborg, a retired judge who still walked the Bergen promenade each morning in a black wool coat. Someone at the fish market had whispered that her late brother once took bribes, a story she had disproved in court decades earlier and never bothered to repeat. Most people shrugged it off. But it reached her niece, who had just been appointed to the bench and who had always believed her uncle was a man without stain. By the next morning, the rumor had found the one door left unlocked, and the niece stopped answering Ingeborg's calls. I, Ingrid, carried the old court file to the niece's office myself, wrapped in brown paper. Ingeborg did not ask whether I had delivered it. She only stood at the railing, watching the gulls ride the wind above the harbor.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “the rumor had found the one door left unlocked” most nearly suggests that the rumor

g.passage: Mumbai was loud that monsoon, but nothing was louder than the quiet at the noodle stall on the corner of Khetwadi Lane. After the mother left for her sister's village and did not return, the old noodle man and his stubborn son kept the stall open as if she had only stepped out for onions. Each night the son set out three bowls, and each night the father filled only two, and neither said a word. Sharda, who sold tea at the next stall, told her niece Priya that the pair were stirring the same pot of silence, and that it would boil over one day. Priya laughed, for the men seemed calm enough. But the tale goes that on the first dry evening of the year, the son set out two bowls, and the father, seeing it, set down his ladle and wept. Steam rose from the pot and drifted toward the lamps.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “stirring the same pot of silence” most nearly suggests that the father and son
options: were too busy preparing food to speak during the crowded evenings.
had quarreled bitterly and refused to work at the same stall again.
were secretly planning together to bring the mother back home.
were jointly keeping up an unspoken avoidance of their loss.
g.explanation: 아들은 매일 그릇 세 개를 놓고 아버지는 두 개만 채우면서도 둘 다 아무 말을 하지 않으며, 어머니가 잠깐 나간 것처럼 가게를 계속 연다. 샤르다가 이를 '같은 침묵의 냄비를 젓는다'고 표현하고 언젠가 끓어 넘칠 것이라 한 것은 두 사람이 상실을 말하지 않고 함께 피하고 있다는 뜻이므로 D가 정답이다. A는 비유를 실제 요리로 읽었고, B는 함께 가게를 지킨다는 서술과 어긋나며, C는 지문에 근거가 없다.
